title: Half the World Is Always Dark
blurb: The sun never rises. Earth rolls you into the light, once every twenty four hours, forever.

blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: The sun does not go out at night. The sun is still shining. Our Earth is round, and it turns. When your side turns toward the sun, you get day. When your side turns away, you get night. Then it turns back around. The sun comes up again. Every day, Earth turns all the way around one time.

blocks.prompt: You Are the One Moving
blocks.text: Earth is a big ball spinning in space. It never stops. It turns all the way around one time every day. The sun stays in one place. It shines all the time. But as Earth turns, your part of the ball swings toward the sun and then away from it. When you face the sun, it is day. When you turn away, it is night. The sun looks like it moves across the sky. It does not. You are the one moving. You are riding on a spinning ball, and you cannot feel it, because everything around you is spinning too.

blocks.prompt: The Line That Never Stops Moving
blocks.text: Stand outside in the morning and watch the sun come up over the edge of the land. It looks like the sun is climbing. It is not. The ground under your feet is tipping you toward it. Earth spins like a ball on a string, one full turn every twenty four hours. Half of the ball is always lit by the sun, and half is always dark. The line between the light half and the dark half has a name. Scientists call it the terminator. That line is always moving, sliding across oceans and cities and mountains, and it never stops. When it slides past you in the morning, you call it sunrise. When it slides past you in the evening, you call it sunset. Somewhere on Earth, right now, someone is watching the sun come up while you are getting ready for bed. It is the same sun. It is the same moment. You are just standing on different parts of a turning ball.

meta.templateLabel: Half the World Is Always Dark

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

blocks.prompt: Why the Sun Rises in the East
blocks.text: If the sun rises in the east every morning, it is worth asking why. The answer has nothing to do with the sun and everything to do with the ground you are standing on. Earth turns on an invisible line called its axis, running from the North Pole to the South Pole. One full turn takes about twenty four hours. At the equator, that spin carries you east at roughly one thousand miles per hour. You feel none of it, because the air, the oceans, your house, and your body are all traveling at the same speed together. Because Earth turns toward the east, the sun appears over the eastern horizon first and sinks below the western one at the end of the day. Sunrise is not the sun arriving. It is you being carried around into the light. There is a second detail that makes days interesting. Earth does not spin upright. It leans by about twenty three degrees. As Earth travels its year long orbit, that lean points the northern half of the planet toward the sun for part of the year and away for the rest. That is why summer days are long and winter days are short, and why the far north can have weeks with no sunset at all while the far south sits in darkness.

5.title: Half the World Is Always Dark
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

meta.templateLabel: Half the World Is Always Dark

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: For most of history, people thought the sun moved
Leon Foucault hung a pendulum in Paris in 1851
You cannot feel steady motion, only changes in motion
The moon's pull acts as a brake on Earth's spin
Days lengthen about 2 milliseconds per century

blocks.prompt: The Proof That Had to Be Built
blocks.text: For most of human history, the obvious explanation was the one that sounded correct. The ground is still. The sun moves. Anyone can watch it happen: sunrise, arc, sunset, repeat. The idea held for thousands of years because it matches exactly what your eyes report. It is wrong, and proving it is harder than it sounds. If Earth spins, why does nothing fly off, why is there no wind rushing past, and why does a dropped ball land at your feet instead of behind you? The answer is that everything near the surface, including the atmosphere and you, is turning along with it. There is no way to feel steady motion. You only feel changes in motion. In 1851, a French physicist named Leon Foucault found a way to show the spin directly. He hung a heavy iron ball on a long wire from a high ceiling in Paris and set it swinging. A swinging pendulum keeps its swing pointed the same way in space. Over the hours, the floor beneath it slowly rotated, and the path of the ball appeared to sweep around the room. Nothing pushed the pendulum. The building, the city, and the country were quietly turning underneath it. Crowds came to watch the planet move. Earth's turn is not perfectly steady either. The moon's gravity pulls on the oceans, and that constant tug acts like a gentle brake. Days are getting longer by roughly two thousandths of a second every century. That is far too small to notice in a lifetime, but the effect adds up over deep time. Fossil corals lay down fine daily growth bands, and corals that lived about four hundred million years ago preserve closer to four hundred bands in a single year. The year was the same length it is now. The days were shorter. Earth was spinning faster then, and it has been slowing ever since.

6.title: Half the World Is Always Dark
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: Half the World Is Always Dark

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: One rotation: about 23 hours 56 minutes against the stars
The terminator sweeps west at over 1,000 mph at the equator
Axial tilt of 23.4 degrees drives the seasons
Circadian clocks keep running in total darkness
Standard time zones were fixed at an 1884 conference
Tidal friction lengthens the day about 2 ms per century

blocks.prompt: The Turning That Makes Everything Else
blocks.text: Every question about day and night comes back to a single fact: Earth turns. It completes one rotation in about twenty four hours, and that rotation carries the surface, the oceans, the atmosphere, and everyone standing on it out of darkness into light and back again. Half the planet faces the sun at any moment and half faces away. The boundary between those halves is called the terminator, and it is never still. Near the equator it sweeps westward at more than a thousand miles per hour, and every sunrise you have ever seen was that line passing over you. Understanding this took a long time, because the evidence of the senses points the other way. The ground feels motionless. The sun visibly travels. Ancient astronomers built careful, mathematically elaborate models in which Earth sat fixed at the center while the heavens wheeled around it, and those models predicted eclipses and planetary positions well enough to survive for well over a thousand years. Being useful is not the same as being true. The rotating Earth won out because it explained more with less, and because instruments eventually caught what the eye could not. Rotation also shapes the day in ways that are easy to miss. Earth's axis is tilted about twenty three and a half degrees away from upright, so as the planet moves along its orbit, one hemisphere leans sunward while the other leans away. This is the entire reason seasons exist, and it is why day length changes through the year. Above the Arctic Circle the tilt is severe enough that the sun refuses to set for weeks in summer and refuses to rise for weeks in winter. Living things track the cycle whether or not they can see it. Nearly every organism studied, from bacteria to trees to humans, runs an internal clock of roughly twenty four hours, and those clocks keep running in constant darkness. The rhythm is not a response to light. It is a prediction of it. The clocks people carry are a much newer invention. For most of history, noon meant the moment the sun stood highest wherever you happened to be standing, which made every town's noon slightly different from its neighbor's. That was tolerable at walking speed and impossible at railway speed. Timetables demanded agreement, so railway companies imposed standard time across the regions they served, and in 1884 an international conference in Washington settled on a single reference line running through Greenwich, England. Time zones are not natural features. They are a treaty laid over a spinning planet. Even the length of the day is negotiable. Tidal friction from the moon acts as a slow brake on Earth's rotation, lengthening the day by roughly two milliseconds per century. Fossil corals record daily growth bands, and specimens from the Devonian period preserve closer to four hundred bands per year, which means the day back then ran near twenty two hours. Atomic clocks now measure the planet's turn precisely enough that timekeepers occasionally insert a leap second to keep official time matched to the actual rotation. The sun has never risen. Earth has only ever rolled you into the light.
